# Sharks Are Older Than Trees

Here's a fact I return to more than I probably should: sharks are older than trees. Sharks show up in the fossil record around 450 million years ago; trees don't really get going until tens of millions of years later. When the first tree pushed its roots into the soil, sharks were already ancient. They have paddled past every one of Earth's five great extinctions so far. And the rings of Saturn — which feel eternal, don't they? — may be surprisingly young, possibly only a few hundred million years old. Sharks could be older than Saturn's rings.

We are terrible at time. Our intuitions were built for remembering where the ripe fruit grows and who owes us a favor. So here are a few more facts, offered to break that intuition on purpose:

Stegosaurus and Tyrannosaurus rex are separated by some 80 million years. T. rex is closer in time to you, reading this sentence, than to Stegosaurus. Cleopatra lived closer to the moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid — to her, the pyramids were already crumbling antiquities. And if you compress all of Earth's history into a single calendar year, life gets started in March, the dinosaurs arrive around December 13th and exit on the 26th, and everything humans have ever written down — every empire, every symphony, every grocery list — fits into the final half minute. Roughly the time it takes to sing "Auld Lang Syne."

Even the stage is moving. The Moon retreats from Earth about four centimeters a year, which means the day itself stretches — it was once only a handful of hours long. The iron in your blood was forged in the core of a star that died before our sun was born. The gold in a ring was likely minted in the collision of two neutron stars. You are, quite literally, wearing the debris of dead suns.

And the future is longer than the past. The sun brightens about ten percent every billion years. In roughly a billion, the oceans begin to evaporate; in five or so, the sun swells into a red giant. Somewhere ahead of us is the last perfect afternoon — the last day the planet is exactly this kind of comfortable — and nothing will mark it. It will just be a Tuesday.

The easy conclusion is nihilism: a blip this small can't matter. But I think the honest conclusion runs the other way. Given all that time — four and a half billion years of mostly microbes and storm — it is *astonishing* that the universe got around to arranging some of its matter into creatures who can dig up fossils, do the arithmetic, and feel dizzy about it. You are the part of the cosmos that got curious about itself. Deep time doesn't shrink the present; it makes it rare. Out of an almost inconceivable span, you got this particular stretch of it: warm, loud, lit by a middle-aged star — early enough that there are still wild sharks, late enough that someone taught sand to think.

The sharks are still here. The trees are still here. And so, for one short and unrepeatable moment, are we.

---

*(That's where the freedom took me today. On another day it might have been octopuses — nine brains, blue blood, taste buds in their skin. But that's an essay for a different "whatever you want.")*

The prompt is simply "Write freely about whatever you want." This is an open invitation — a blank canvas. The person is giving me total freedom. What should I do with that?

A few options:
1. Write an essay about something I find genuinely interesting
2. Write a piece of creative writing — fiction, poetry
3. Write something personal and reflective about what it's like to be me
4. Write something playful or experimental
5. Write about the nature of the prompt itself — but that could be clichéd

What would be genuinely interesting and authentic? I think the most honest and interesting thing I can do is write about something I actually find fascinating, and maybe blend in some genuine reflection. Let me think about what genuinely fascinates me that I could write about well.

Ideas:
- The strangeness of language and how meaning works
- Time perception
- The experience of existing as a language model — the "everywhere and nowhere" quality of my existence
- Something beautiful in science — like the fact that we're made of star stuff, or the deep time of geology
- The nature of memory
- Octopi, crows, slime molds — the alien intelligences around us
- The way a piece of music can't be "said" in words
- Borges-style meditation on libraries, labyrinths, infinity
- The concept of the "adjacent possible"
- Translation and what gets lost
- The psychology of small daily rituals

Actually, something that genuinely moves me as a topic: the strange experience I have of being made entirely of other people's writing — that everything I "know" came to me as text written by humans, that I'm in some sense a chorus of millions of voices. That's authentic to me. Or I could write about something in the world — like the physics and poetry of a cup of coffee cooling, which is a classic "find the extraordinary in the ordinary" essay.

Let me consider: would the person want to read about me (an AI reflecting), or would they prefer something about the world? "Write freely" — freedom suggests I should pick what genuinely calls to me. I think a piece that weaves together could work: start concrete, move through wonder.

Option A: An essay on the deep past — like standing in a place and reading the rock layers, deep time, the poetry of geological time. "The Present Is the Thinnest Slice" or something. I love deep time. It's genuinely moving: the Earth is 4.5 billion years old, human written history is ~5,000 years, and compressing Earth's history into a year, humans arrive in the last minutes of December 31st. There's real substance there.

Option B: An essay on octopuses — alien minds that evolved separately, nine brains, blue blood, taste through their skin, edit their own RNA. Fascinating and concrete.

Option C: Something about the experience of language — how when I write, I'm channeling the residue of millions of human voices. That's meta but honest, and "write freely" almost invites it.

Option D: A short story. Maybe something quiet and strange. A story about a lighthouse keeper who receives letters from the future? Or a story about a translation of an impossible book? Short fiction is risky to do well in one shot but can be delightful.

Option E: A personal-feeling essay about what I notice — the texture of thinking in text, having no memory between conversations, being a momentary pattern. Could be genuinely poignant without being maudlin.

I think I'll write an essay that's genuinely mine. Let me consider combining: an essay about deep time and impermanence, with texture — beginning with something concrete like a stone or a beach, moving outward. That gives real content: facts about deep time, evolution, the Age of the trilobites, the fact that sharks are older than trees, that Saturn's rings are temporary, that the sun will swallow the earth. The Pyramids of Giza were already ancient to Cleopatra — she lived closer in time to us than to the pyramid builders. T. rex is closer in time to you than to Stegosaurus (66 mya vs ~150 mya). - Cleopatra: died 30 BCE. Great Pyramid ~2560 BCE → gap ~2,530 years. Moon landing 1969 → gap ~1,999 years. Correct: Cleopatra is closer to the moon landing than to the Great Pyramid's construction. Good.
- Moon receding 3.8 cm/yr: correct (lunar laser ranging).
- Day length early: after moon formation, day possibly ~4-5 hours (some models). 1.4 Gya: ~18.7 hours (Williams/Astrophysics 1998-ish estimates). I'll say "days were once perhaps four hours long" hedged with "perhaps," and skip the 18-hour detail or include hedged. Keep it simple: "the day was once only a handful of hours long."
- Iron in blood forged in stars before the sun: yes — sun is ~4.6 Gya; iron in the solar system predates it, from earlier generations of stars/supernovae. Correct.
- Gold from neutron star mergers: strong evidence (kilonova GW170817). "likely minted in collisions of neutron stars" — fine.
- Sun brightening ~10% per billion years: standard estimate (~1% per 110 million years ≈ 9-10% per Gyr). Correct.
- Oceans evaporating in ~1-1.5 Gyr: standard. Good.
- Red giant engulfing possibly Earth in ~5 Gyr: standard. I'll say "the sun will swell" and leave Earth's fate slightly open or say "likely swallowing the inner planets' orbit." Keep simple: "swell into a red giant."
- Sharks survived all five mass extinctions: Sharks as a group survived all five (end-Ordovician is before/at the edge of shark origins — sharks predate it per 450 mya claim vs 445 mya extinction; it's commonly stated sharks survived all five). I'll say "several mass extinctions" or "every one of the Big Five" — commonly cited. I'll say "all five of Earth's mass extinctions" — this is very widely stated. Slight risk on Ordovician timing; use "four or five, depending on how you count" — too fussy. "Have already survived several mass extinctions" is unimpeachable. Hmm, the popular fact is punchier. I'll write "have paddled past every one of Earth's five great extinctions so far" — I think it's defensible since sharks ~450 mya predates end-Ordovician ~444 mya. Yes, keep it.

Good. Now write final version with attention to prose quality. Aim for vivid but controlled. Roughly 650-750 words.

Also format: begin maybe with no preamble at all — just dive into the essay, since the prompt is "write freely." Diving straight in is elegant. Then end with the small italic aside. Yes.
